abstract: While protein-folding software has made great strides in recent years, reliability is known to be poorer on novel structures and failure modes are not fully characterised. Cancer fusion proteins present a unique case of proteins absent from model training data but constructed from parents with known structures. This study tests four popular protein-folding tools on three categories of protein: control, cancer-associated, and uncharacterised fusion proteins. We assessed computational performance, accuracy, and distinct failure modes. For well-characterised proteins, all tools tested returned the correct structures in all but one case, with some tools returning an average of two distinct structural forms in the exception. For characterised cancer-associated proteins, most predictions were highly accurate; poorer predictions often still returned some consistent high-confidence domains but produced divergent results in other areas that were both variable between tools and at odds with experimental structures. For cancer fusion proteins having available parent-protein reference structures, results fell into two clear categories. Roughly half contained structures matching to the functional domains of their parent proteins at high confidence, in keeping with biological expectation for these proteins; the others contained little evidence of matching structures, independent of the tool used. Predictions for fusion proteins differed far more between tools than those for characterised proteins with a median inter-tool TM-score 0.272 versus 0.853 respectively. However, agreement between tools did not indicate a more biologically plausible prediction. For example, all tools predicted drastically different structures for fusion protein TMPRSS2-ERG, but all predictions still contained the core ERG functional domains; conversely, all tools produced highly consistent structures for DNAJB1-PRKACA, but none of the predictions contained the expected functional regions. We recommend that users of these tools use care and caution in the assessments of outputs and consider biological knowledge before blindly trusting results.
